items.title: Wycliffe Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001
items.q: there’s a jam session that takes place in New York the first Monday of every month at this sculpture’s house, Clint Meadmore.

ctx.x: I think that it’s happening. It’s kind of hard to tell because I’m not one that — most of the time when I travel I’m in my room working on music so I don’t get the chance to interact with a lot of musicians. But it’s been, I think it’s kind of like a catch 22. There are those of us that try to stick together and support one another in the name, in the spirit of what the older musicians would do because I feel like there was a generation of musicians where that existed. And that could have been like Sweets…

Britt Woodman. And then came the bebop period and not that all the guys took on this, but I think that it became more of a me-thing. It became more of music for the musicians. And not that non-musicians couldn’t listen to it, but I think there was a social element in the music during the Swing Era where people would get together and go listen to the music because they didn’t just have to sit down and listen at a concert, they could dance with the music and it had a social element that invited everyone. And I…
It’s all right. I like this subject.
